The Fisher King Gilliam was to continue his exploration of reality versus unreality in his next film, The Fisher King.

A film I have mixed feelings about due to the obvious impact of Robin Williams' notorious sentimentality.

The Fisher King is quite different from the rest of Gilliam's movies. He deliberately wanted a smaller and quieter movie after the chaos and commercial issues surrounding Baron Munchausen.

This is the first of his films where Gilliam wasn't involved in the screenplay. The film is significant because it shows a level of maturity in Gilliam's progress as a director.

It was the first of his films to not cast a fellow Python member, though there is still the Holy Grail connection.

After this film though, we can say Gilliam reached independence. Despite the Holy Grail connection, the film is fairly grounded in the real world except for the titular character's hallucinations surrounding the Grail.

It is at heart a quite ordinary story grounded in the real world. To summarize, the plot involves Jeff Bridges as a radio shock jock whose chat show inadvertently causes a gunman to carry out a shooting in a crowded New York restaurant.

This sends the DJ into a depressive spiral who then loses his job and moves in above a video store.

Three years later, the rock bottom former DJ encounters a crazy homeless guy played by Robin Williams who stops him from committing suicide.

Williams is a fantasist obsessed with finding the Holy Grail that he is convinced lies hidden in New York.

Boiling the rest of the plot, the story is relatively normie fair. It is Gilliam's most mainstream film besides Brothers Grimm.
